actual_assessment:
Working preference: K, “the earth heaves before him,” for this restricted English comparison. I would select K within the supplied pair rather than HOLD the pairwise decision. Because candidate identities are masked, I cannot say whether selecting K entails retaining or changing the existing text.

Both candidates make the earth the grammatical subject of an intransitive movement expression and locate that response before the divine presence. Neither explicitly introduces an agent lifting the earth, its destruction, its removal, or a required literal geological event. This is compatible with the packet’s declared analysis of retained נשׂא, while the unusual intransitive usage leaves the precise English movement sense uncertain.

K’s “heaves” presents a powerful, unsettled movement of the earth. In the supplied paragraph, that coheres with mountains quaking, hills melting, waters drying, and rocks being shattered. It also accommodates the earth/world/inhabitants expansion as a poetic description of the whole inhabited order responding to judgment. The wording is readable and forceful.

The strongest objection to K is that “heaves” can narrow the movement toward convulsion, swelling, or upheaval. The packet’s lifting/rising gloss does not independently establish that particular sense. Context makes “heaves” plausible; it does not demonstrate it. K also loses the explicit “face” image and the immediately recognizable upward sense of “rises.”

R’s “rises up” more transparently expresses the packet’s lifting/rising interpretation. It leaves open a broad poetic elevation of the inhabited order and could create an effective English echo with the following question, “who can rise up.” That is a literary observation about the supplied English context, not evidence that the underlying Hebrew expressions share a lexeme.

R’s main drawback is that “rises up before his face” can suggest an erect, confronting, or actively opposing world. It does not assert rebellion, but the English phrase permits that association more readily than K. “Up” also makes upward movement explicit, whereas the supplied evidence does not settle the unusual verb’s precise contextual sense. “Before his face” preserves the anthropomorphic lexical image but is less natural English and can encourage readers to picture a spatial encounter with a bodily face.

Neither candidate fully preserves the close gloss’s “from/before” range. Both choose presence language, and R’s literal “face” does not restore the possible source/separation nuance. A note could preserve the face wording, the lifting/rising interpretation, and the uncertainty of the unusual intransitive construction. The alternative repointing as an apocopated Niphal of שׁאה should remain disclosed as a separate textual interpretation; it cannot decide this comparison under unchanged pointing.

Under DOCTRINE.md, K has the better overall balance of intelligibility, rhetorical force, and restrained English implication, although R has the stronger immediate lexical transparency. My preference depends on treating “heaves” as poetic movement, without certifying a convulsive or geological mechanism. If that movement sense cannot be supported beyond the supplied contextual argument, HOLD would be appropriate before presenting K as a settled interpretation.

Reversing the order to R followed by K does not change my reasoning or preference. R’s lexical transparency remains its principal strength, and K’s contextual force and naturalness remain the reasons for choosing it. This order check is part of this single assessment, not an independent vote.

This is an interpretation and English assessment using only the supplied packet and the specified doctrine sections. It is not new primary-source consultation, fresh decipherment, a finding about original pointing priority, or certification of a unique or whole-verse optimum.
